title: Vayera: here am I (Genesis 22:1, 7, 11)
hook: Abraham answers "here am I" to God, to his son and to the angel
tomorrow: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac was born, and Sarah's laugh turned from doubt to joy. Your line was laugh with me. Today, the last day of Vayera, and its hardest chapter.

Someone calls your name from the next room. Yeah? What? In a minute. Half your mind is still on what you were doing. Now think of the few times you answered with all of you. A child crying at night, and you're up before you're awake. A friend on the phone, and you hear that something's wrong, so you put everything down. Hebrew has a word for answering like that. It's not just yes. It means: I'm here, fully. Abraham says it three times in one chapter.
screen: `YEAH? WHAT? IN A MINUTE.` → `ANSWERING WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The word is hineni. Here I am. The chapter is Genesis twenty-two, which Jews call the Akedah, the binding of Isaac. Jewish readers have argued over it for a long time. It begins: "God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'" God tells him to take his son, his only son, whom he loves, Isaac, and offer him up on a mountain. Abraham rises early and goes. On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain together, Isaac carrying the wood. Isaac speaks: "My father." And Abraham says: "Here am I, my son." The same word. Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham says God will provide. At the top, when Abraham has bound Isaac and taken up the knife, an angel calls from heaven: Abraham, Abraham. A third time he answers: here am I. Don't lay your hand on the boy, the angel says. Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead. Isaac is not harmed. Readers disagree deeply about this story. Some see Abraham's complete faith. Some read it as a rejection of child sacrifice. Some modern readers ask why the man who argued for Sodom says nothing here. Whatever they make of it, they keep coming back to the word. Hineni, to God. Hineni, to his son. Hineni, to the angel who stops him. Fully present to each. Later, when God calls, the prophet Isaiah will answer: "Here am I; send me." So that's Vayera: a visit to the sick, an argument for justice, a stranger's goodness, a laugh of joy, and here am I.
screen: `GOD CALLS: HERE AM I.` · `ISAAC CALLS: HERE AM I, MY SON.` · `THE ANGEL CALLS: HERE AM I.` · `READERS DISAGREE DEEPLY.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Silently say: here I am, and notice where you actually are: your body, this room, this moment. Then think of someone who might call your name, a child, a parent, a friend, a coworker, and picture answering not with in a minute, but with all of you. If you pray, you can say it to God too.
Hineni. Here I am: not just yes, but fully present, Abraham's answer to God, to his son, and to the angel.
Your line: here I am. Three calls, one answer, all of him. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The binding of Isaac, the Akedah, is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and some Jews recite it in the daily morning prayers; hineni is also the name of a prayer the cantor says before the additional (Musaf) service on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in some communities.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording and punctuation of Genesis 22:1, 22:7 ('My father.' / 'Here am I, my son.') and Isaiah 6:8.

Readings of the Akedah given side by side without ranking: supreme faith; rejection of child sacrifice (a common modern reading); midrashic wondering whether Abraham should have argued. Confirm fairness and whether a specific midrash should be cited for the third.
'Which other peoples of the time practiced' (child sacrifice in the ancient Near East): stated briefly; confirm the phrasing is careful enough.
The Akedah in the daily morning service and on the second day of Rosh Hashanah; the cantor's Hineni prayer (Ashkenazi High Holiday rite): confirm.

Reviewer edits: 'which other peoples of the time practiced' softened to 'which some neighboring peoples are thought to have practiced' (extent of ancient Near Eastern child sacrifice is debated); howItsDone now places the cantor's Hineni before Musaf. Confirm.

'Isaac is not harmed' follows the plain text; some midrashim (e.g. traditions that Isaac's ashes or blood were shed, or that he was taken to Eden) read otherwise. Keeper to decide whether to acknowledge.
